name: Stem Separation and Restoration
title: Stem Separation and Restoration
answer: Stem separation and restoration covers isolating individual instrumental or vocal parts from a mixed recording and repairing degraded audio such as noise, clipping, dropouts, or missing spectral content. It is used in remixing, mastering, archival recovery, film and game audio, and music education. The field sits within music composition and audio engineering, where the goal is often to recover usable multitrack material from a finished stereo or mono master. Restoration also includes removing hum, clicks, and broadband noise while preserving the musical signal.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Modern stem separation typically runs on local workstations with a dedicated GPU, though some services run in the cloud. Restoration tasks can often run on a CPU for shorter files, but batch work and high-resolution audio benefit from GPU acceleration. Models are usually delivered as plugins, standalone applications, or Python libraries that process audio offline rather than in real time. Latency is less critical than fidelity, so engineers often run separation as a pre-processing step before a mix session.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done with neural networks trained on large collections of mixed audio and their isolated stems. A common approach is to use a U-Net or a transformer that takes a spectrogram of the mix and outputs masks or magnitude estimates for each target source, such as vocals, drums, bass, and other. Restoration models learn to map corrupted audio to clean audio, often using paired examples of degraded and pristine recordings. The output is then converted back to a waveform with a phase reconstruction step, which can introduce subtle artifacts that an engineer must check.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk center on who may separate stems from a recording and what they may do with the results. Separating a copyrighted song can create derivative works, and using separated stems in a new production without permission may infringe the rights of the original performers, songwriters, or label. Restoration of archival material raises provenance questions, because a cleaned transfer may be mistaken for an original master if the processing chain is not documented. Some AI music services face active intellectual property lawsuits, and 18 of the 92 tracked suits involve AI music services, which shows that courts are still settling how training data and separated output are treated. This is not legal advice, but practitioners should keep clear records of source material and permissions.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Stem separation is moving toward real-time or near-real-time operation, which would let live sound engineers isolate and adjust sources during a performance. Restoration is likely to improve at reconstructing missing audio, such as filling gaps from tape damage or recovering lost harmonics, rather than only suppressing noise. Models are also becoming more controllable, with text or reference-based prompts that let an engineer specify which instrument to keep or what kind of clean signal to target. The practical limit remains the quality of the original recording, because no model can fully recover information that was never captured.
